14	CASE OD2-DEV2-INTERACT (INTERACT, technical): Larkfield DC: robot collision stops tripled in September

18	E1 [stage S1] Fleet management system, weekly safety KPI extract (system-record): Larkfield DC: protective ('collision') stops, all 58 HR-7 robots, by ISO week 2026: wk30 201, wk31 209, wk32 198, wk33 212, wk34 207, wk35 203, wk36 412, wk37 640, wk38 655, wk39 662, wk40 648, wk41 651. 21	E4 [stage S1] Email from Halvane Robotics Customer Support (Tier 2), 25 September (vendor-account): 'We've reviewed your ticket. 22	E5 [stage S1] Interview notes, R. Comparison row for the same weeks in 2025: cut-off misses rose from 2 to 7 per week during that peak, while collision stops stayed near 200 per week. Dashboard note: robot stop time is not linked to wave completion data.
24	CATALOGUE (full contents)
25	C1 [stage S1] Collision-stop event log with badge-tag proximity field, weeks 30–41 - Fleet management system export with HR roster note (log): Each stop record shows the nearest UWB badge tag within 3 m at the moment of the stop. 26	C2 [stage S1] Collision-stop rates by firmware group and zone, weeks 33–41 - Site engineering analysis of fleet telemetry (telemetry): Stops per 100 robot-hours, weeks 33–35 compared with weeks 37–41. 38	C14 [stage S1] Site safety committee minutes, 8 October - Safety committee secretary (document): Item 3, vendor proposal to shorten the protective field by 20%: site risk assessment RA-114 sets the current field length as the minimum for mixed pedestrian and robot lanes at 1.2 m/s. The item was referred to the GM for decision.
39	C15 [stage S1] Fleet configuration and map change history, July–October - Fleet manager audit trail (change-record): Map edits: two charging stations moved in Zone C in week 31. 41	H1: The September fleet firmware update, on its own, caused the rise in collision stops.
42	H2: The August change of outbound pallet stretch film, on its own, caused the rise in collision stops.
43	H3: Seasonal agency temps entering robot lanes caused the rise in collision stops.
44	H4: The September firmware update and the August film change together caused the rise in collision stops; neither would have produced it alone.
45	H5: The September firmware update and the arrival of the agency temps together caused the rise in collision stops; neither would have produced it alone.
46	H6: Halvane's planned December release would, on its own, bring stop rates back to the pre-September level while the current film stays in use.
47	R1: Fleet firmware update from 6.3 to 6.4 (2–4 September) -> Tripling of weekly collision stops (contributes to)
48	R2: Switch to the new outbound stretch film (August) -> Tripling of weekly collision stops (contributes to)
49	R3: Arrival of 46 agency temps on the floor (31 August) -> Tripling of weekly collision stops (contributes to)
50	R4: Tripling of weekly collision stops -> Rise in missed carrier cut-offs (contributes to)
51	A1: Switch outbound pallets back to the previous supplier's stretch film, keep all robots on their current firmware, and track weekly stop rates by zone and firmware group against the September–October figures.

53	A3: Accept Halvane's offer to shorten the protective field by 20% on all robots to cut stop frequency during peak.

answers.justification: The 6.4 tote robots in Zone C, where no wrapped pallets are staged, stayed flat at 2.4 to 2.5 (C2). In the bench test, 6.4 with the old matte film stopped 0/20 times (C3), and other 6.4 sites show no rise (C7), so firmware alone does not explain the increase.

The gloss film was in use from 4–11 August, yet stops stayed near 200 per week until week 36 (E1, E5, C9). The 6.3 robots in A/B stayed flat at 3.1 to 3.3 (C2), and 6.3 with gloss film stopped only 1/20 times on the bench (C3).

Stops with a badge tag nearby barely changed (41 to 44), while stops with no tag nearby rose from 164 to 607, and 99.2% of floor entries were tagged (C1). The temps were spread across all zones, yet only 6.4 robots in A/B rose (C1, C2), and the training records are clean (C4).

Only 6.4 robots working near gloss-wrapped pallets rose (3.2 to 15.6), while robots with one factor alone stayed flat (C2). The bench test showed 17/20 stops for 6.4 with gloss, against 1/20 and 0/20 for the other combinations, with no people present (C3), and the engineer described the mechanism (C3, C8).
The temps were also in Zone C, where the 6.4 robots stayed flat, and tagged stops did not rise (C1, C2). The bench test reproduced the stops with no people present (C3).

Release 6.4.2 is meant to reclassify the film reflections, but it has not been tested against this film (C3, E4), so the evidence neither confirms nor rules out that it would fix the problem on its own.

The eight robots left on 6.3 act as a natural control under the same dynamic mission assignment (C2). The bench intervention (C3) and the near-field filtering mechanism (E3, C3) show that firmware contributes, though only together with the film.

In the bench test with 6.4, switching from matte to gloss film raised stops from 0/20 to 17/20 (C3). Gloss is 90 vs 55 GU (C8), and the rise appeared only in the pallet zones (C2), so the film contributes through its interaction with 6.4.

Tagged stops stayed flat at about 41–44 per week (C1). The temps were spread across zones while the rise was confined to 6.4 robots in A/B (C1, C2), and contact and near-miss reports were unchanged (C10).

Missed waves had more stops (median 61 against 49), but they were also the largest waves, and the analyst has not separated volume from stops (C11). In 2025, cut-off misses rose from 2 to 7 per week with no rise in stops (E6), and wait time is not recorded per wave.

The matte film gave 0/20 stops with 6.4 (C3). The old film can be ordered within three working days (C9), and this option keeps 6.4's security patches and thin-obstacle detection (E3, C3) without touching the safety configuration.

6.3 with gloss film produced few stops (C2, C3), so a rollback would likely work. However, 6.3 security support ends 31 October (E3), the rollback gives up 6.4's thin-obstacle detection (C3), and the film switch (C9) is a cheaper, cleaner remedy.

Risk assessment RA-114 sets the current field as the minimum for mixed lanes at 1.2 m/s, and the safety committee did not endorse a cut (C14), so shortening the field would weaken a protective control.

The stops are caused by firmware and film, not by people (C1, C2, C3), and the temps' training records are clean (C4). Matching stops to rosters would punish the wrong people (C14), and E2's dismissal of the firmware is wrong.

Release 6.4.2 has not been tested against this film (C3) and is not due until December (E4), so committing to it as the permanent fix depends on H6, which is unconfirmed, while the stops continue through peak.

The natural experiment by firmware group and zone (C2), the bench intervention (C3), and the elimination of temps, network and maintenance causes (C1, C5, C6, C15) are enough to commit to the low-risk, reversible film switch (A1).

ambiguousItems: S12: rolling back to 6.3 could also be called premature or harmful, because 6.3 security support ends 31 Oct (E3) and 6.4's improved fork-tine detection would be lost (C3); 'acceptable' is also defensible because it would cut the stops (C2, C3).
S15: an indefinite wait for an untested fix during peak could also be called harmful, but 'premature' fits better.
S10: 'unknown' is also defensible, since robot wait time is not recorded per wave (C11).
caseProblems: C3's catalogue title ('Bench test of protective stops against staged outbound pallets') and C2's grouping by firmware and zone point strongly toward the answer, but they do not state it outright.
C3 is a near-perfect 2x2 factorial in which the field engineer explains the mechanism directly, which makes the interaction case unusually clean.
E5's technician argument against the film is set up as a deliberate decoy that the interaction resolves. This is realistic, but it should be noted.
